style_2_guidelines.guideline_authority: ACR Guidelines for Rheumatic Diseases & EULAR Consensus (2024)

clinical_targets.goal: Normalization of serum CRP and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Halt radiographic joint erosion and preserve physical mobility

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Chest Injuries and Disorders focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Chest Injuries and Disorders require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Chest Injuries and Disorders.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Avoid NSAIDs in eGFR < 30 mL/min; adjust methotrexate and allopurinol based on renal clearance.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Screen for hepatitis B/C before starting DMARDs or biologics; monitor ALT/AST with methotrexate.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Methotrexate and leflunomide are strictly contraindicated; certolizumab and hydroxychloroquine are preferred.
special_populations.elderly: High risk of NSAID-induced gastrointestinal ulcers, fluid retention, and acute kidney injury; co-prescribe PPI.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is the chest? The chest is the part of your body between your neck and your abdomen (belly). The medical term for your chest is thorax. Your chest holds many important structures for breathing, digestion, blood circulation, and other important body functions. These structures include your: Ribs and breastbone Esophagus, the tube between your mouth and stomach Trachea, your windpipe Bronchi, the tubes that carry air from your windpipe to your lungs Lungs Pleura, a thin layer of tissue that covers the lungs and lines the inside wall of the chest space Heart and large blood vessels Thymus, a gland that's part of your immune system Nerves What are chest injuries and disorders? Chest injuries and disorders are problems that affect any of the organs or structures located in your chest. There are many types of chest injuries and disorders, for example: Broken ribs Esophagus disorders Swallowing disorders , also called dysphagia Tracheal disorders Bronchial disorders Lung diseases and collapsed lung Pleural disorders Heart diseases Mediastinal diseases, which are tumors, inflammation, and other problems with the structures in the mediastinum, which is the space between your lungs, breastbone, and spine Thoracic aortic aneurysm Thoracic outlet syndrome Chest injuries may happen from the force of car accidents, falls , or sports injuries . Or the chest may be pierced by a bullet or sharp object. Because your chest holds so many important structures, certain chest injuries may be life-threatening. How are chest injuries and disorders diagnosed? Diagnosis of chest injuries or disorders depends on the type of symptoms you're having and whether you've had a chest injury. Injuries are usually obvious, but in most cases, you'll need tests to know how serious an injury is. There are many types of tests for diagnosing different types of chest injuries and disorders, for example: Diagnostic imaging tests Heart tests Lung function tests Bronchoscopy Pleural fluid analysis Dysphagia tests Biopsy Treatments will depend on the type of chest injury or disorder you have.
style_3_monograph.treatment: Consult healthcare provider for individualized management.
